screens.title: What is a CDN and how CloudFront uses edge locations
screens.narratorSegment: A CDN is a distributed system that stores copies of content closer to users to lower latency and handle more traffic without overwhelming the origin. In CloudFront, those caches live at edge locations worldwide. Think of a CDN like a network of neighborhood libraries: instead of every reader traveling to a single central archive, the city keeps copies nearby so most readers get instant access. For a developer this matters because your static assets—images, stylesheets, scripts—and even some dynamic responses can be served directly from those edge caches. That reduces round-trip time, speeds page loads, and lowers origin costs. A clear example: a user in Tokyo requesting an image stored in an S3 bucket in Virginia will be served from the nearest edge if cached, avoiding the transoceanic trip to the origin. A common misconception is that CDNs always serve the latest version; they do not unless you configure short TTLs or invalidate items. TTLs and cache-control headers control freshness, so plan for update workflows, staging, and invalidation as part of your deployment process. Remember that a CDN is not just performance—it's also a layer where security and request filtering can be applied before origin resources are touched.

keyIdea.text: A CDN stores cached copies of content at edge locations to serve users with lower latency and less origin load.

content.html:
Core Concept CDN Definition
What is a CDN and why it matters
Edge caching explained with an everyday analogy and developer implications.
Analogy
A CDN is like neighborhood libraries holding copies of books so readers don't travel to the central archive.
Developer example
An app serving static files from S3 will return images from the edge for most users, cutting latency and origin bandwidth.
Common mistake
Assuming cached objects are always fresh; without TTLs or invalidation you may serve stale assets.
What happens on a request
  • Client requests an object. CloudFront checks the nearest edge location cache.
  • If present and fresh, CloudFront serves the cached object immediately.
  • If missing or expired, CloudFront fetches from the configured origin and caches the response per policy.
Key Takeaway

Edge caching improves performance and resilience; manage TTLs and invalidations to control freshness.

screens.title: CloudFront distribution, origins, and behaviors
screens.narratorSegment: A CloudFront distribution is the configuration object that connects viewers to origins. Each distribution can have multiple origins: think of an S3 bucket for static files, an Application Load Balancer for dynamic application traffic, and even a custom HTTP server. Behaviors define which origin serves a given URL path and which caching settings apply. For example, a behavior for /images/* can point to an S3 origin with long TTLs and allow only GET and HEAD methods, while /api/* maps to an ALB with all methods allowed and minimal caching. Viewer protocol policy within a behavior enforces whether HTTP requests are redirected to HTTPS. Origin request policies let you control which headers, cookies, and query strings CloudFront forwards to the origin — this affects cache key granularity. A practical rule: keep cache keys as small as possible to increase cache hit rates. Also, when an ALB or EC2 is used as an origin, verify security group and network rules so CloudFront can reach the origin. This architecture separates static and dynamic concerns while improving global performance and operational control. CloudFront distribution, origins, and behaviors means a distribution ties multiple origins to path-based behaviors, each with its own caching and protocol rules.. In practical terms, how distributions map user requests to the right origin and caching policy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Architecture Distribution & Behaviors
Distributions, origins and behaviors
Map URL paths to origins and choose caching and protocol policies.
Origins (examples)
  • S3 bucket for static assets like images and JavaScript.
  • Application Load Balancer for dynamic API or server-rendered pages.
  • Custom HTTP origin for legacy servers or third-party content.
Behavior settings
  • Path pattern (for example, /images/* or /api/*).
  • Allowed HTTP methods and viewer protocol policy.
  • Cache and origin request policies defining TTL and forwarded values.
Example behavior mapping
/images/* → S3 origin. Long TTL. GET/HEAD only.
/api/* → ALB origin. Minimal caching. All methods forwarded.
/stream/* → MediaStore or MediaPackage origin. Streaming optimized.
Key Takeaway

Behaviors let you treat each URL pattern with the right origin and cache policy to balance freshness and speed.

screens.title: Caching strategies and cache-control headers
screens.narratorSegment: Caching strategy is the set of decisions that determine how long objects remain in edge caches and when to fetch fresh content from an origin. CloudFront uses cache policies and origin headers to build cache keys and set TTL behavior. Start by choosing what to include in the cache key: ideally, keep it minimal so more requests match the same cache entry. Headers, cookies, and query strings can be forwarded selectively; forward only what your origin needs. TTLs are defined as minimum, default, and maximum values in cache policies. Use long TTLs for versioned static assets and shorter TTLs for frequently changing resources. Set Cache-Control and Expires headers on the origin to communicate freshness; CloudFront honors those unless overridden by distribution cache policy. A common workflow is to deploy new static files with versioned filenames, set long TTLs, and then avoid invalidations. When you cannot version, use targeted invalidations for changed paths. A common pitfall is over-broad forwarding of headers or caching keys leading to cache fragmentation and poor hit ratio. Balance precision and simplicity to maximize cache effectiveness and reduce origin load.

keyIdea.text: Minimize cache-key variance, set TTLs appropriate to content volatility, and use versioning to avoid frequent invalidations.

content.html:
Process Flow Caching Strategy
Design caching and cache keys
How TTLs, headers and cache keys affect hit rates and freshness.
Step-by-step
  1. Decide what elements form the cache key: path, selected headers, cookies, query strings.
  2. Set cache policy TTLs: min, default, max based on update frequency.
  3. Use origin headers like Cache-Control to fine-tune behavior when possible.
  4. Prefer asset versioning for long TTLs to avoid invalidations.
Practical examples
Versioned script: /js/app.v2.1.0.js — use long TTL.
API response: /api/user/profile — short TTL or no cache and forward auth headers.
Common mistake
Forwarding too many headers or cookies fragments the cache and reduces hit ratios. Forward only necessary values.

screens.title: Cache invalidation and automation (code example)
screens.narratorSegment: Cache invalidation forces CloudFront to remove specified objects from edge caches before their TTL expires so that subsequent requests fetch the updated content from the origin. Use invalidations sparingly and target specific paths to preserve cache benefits. A common automated pattern is to call the SDK as part of a CI/CD pipeline after deploying new static assets. The provided Python example shows how to create an invalidation for one or more paths using the CloudFront client. The function builds an InvalidationBatch with a unique caller reference and a list of paths. In practice, call this function only for changed files or a narrow prefix like /assets/css/* rather than invalidating the entire distribution. A misconception is that invalidation updates all edge caches instantly — invalidation removes items so edges will fetch fresh content on next request, and propagation can take time. Also, frequent or broad invalidations can incur costs or negate caching performance. Automate targeted invalidations for versionless assets and prefer filename versioning to avoid invalidation where possible. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Invalidation
keyIdea.text: Use SDK calls to create targeted invalidations after deployments; avoid broad wildcards to retain cache benefits.

content.html:
Process Flow Invalidation via SDK
Programmatic invalidation example
Use targeted invalidations from your automation system after asset deployment.
When to invalidate
  • After deploying non-versioned static files that must be visible immediately.
  • To remove cached config or assets that cause functional regressions.
  • Never use broad invalidation unless necessary due to cost and performance impact.
Pro Tip

Prefer filename versioning for static assets to reduce the need for invalidation.

Python example
import boto3
import time

cloudfront = boto3.client('cloudfront', region_name='us-east-1')

def invalidate_cloudfront_paths(distribution_id, paths):
  """
  Invalidates specified paths in a CloudFront distribution.
  Paths should start with '/'. Example: ['/index.html', '/css/*']
  """
  try:
    response = cloudfront.create_invalidation(
      DistributionId=distribution_id,
      InvalidationBatch={
        'Paths': {
          'Quantity': len(paths),
          'Items': paths
        },
        'CallerReference': str(time.time())
      }
    )
    print(f"Successfully initiated CloudFront invalidation: {response['Invalidation']['Id']}")
    return response['Invalidation']['Id']
  except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error initiating invalidation: {e}")
    return None

# Example usage: invalidate_cloudfront_paths('E123ABCDEFGH', ['/index.html', '/assets/*'])

screens.title: Securing CloudFront: TLS, WAF, and Origin Access Control
screens.narratorSegment: Security for content delivery has multiple layers. First, encrypt traffic between users and CloudFront by attaching a TLS certificate from AWS Certificate Manager to the distribution. Use a viewer protocol policy to redirect HTTP to HTTPS so all viewers connect securely. Second, protect the distribution from common web exploits by attaching AWS WAF rules — for example, blocking S Q L injection or limiting requests from suspicious IP ranges. WAF operates at the edge and reduces malicious traffic before it reaches origins. Third, when using S3 as an origin, prevent direct public access by using Origin Access Control. OAC (or the older OAI) ensures the bucket accepts requests only from CloudFront; update the bucket policy as instructed when creating the OAC. This prevents bypassing CloudFront and ensures that WAF, signed URLs, and other distribution-wide protections are always applied. Also consider signed URLs or signed cookies when you must restrict content to authorized users for a limited time. Overall, combine these layers to enforce encryption, filter threats, and lock down origin access. Securing CloudFront: TLS, WAF, and Origin Access Control means use tls for encryption, waf for filtering, and oac to restrict s3 so all requests go through cloudfront protections.. In practical terms, protecting data in transit, filtering traffic, and preventing direct origin access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Security TLS, WAF & OAC
Secure your distribution end-to-end
Encrypt, filter, and lock down origin access so content is delivered safely.
TLS with ACM
Attach an AWS Certificate Manager certificate to serve content over HTTPS. Enforce HTTPS with viewer protocol policy to avoid mixed content.
AWS WAF
Apply rules at the edge to block common attack patterns before they reach your origins, reducing load and exposure.
Origin Access Control
Use OAC so the S3 bucket accepts requests only from CloudFront, preventing direct bucket access and bypass of WAF or signed URLs.
Key Takeaway

Combine TLS, WAF, and OAC to ensure encrypted, filtered, and authorized delivery through CloudFront.

screens.title: Signed URLs and Signed Cookies for restricted content
screens.narratorSegment: Signed URLs and signed cookies are the mechanisms CloudFront provides to control access to private content. They let your application issue time-limited, cryptographically signed requests that CloudFront validates before serving the object. Use signed URLs for individual resources when you want a single link to expire, and signed cookies when you need to give a browser access to multiple restricted files without signing each URL. Implementing signed access typically requires a private key to sign policy statements that include resource path and expiration. The origin remains private — in the case of S3, you combine signed URLs with Origin Access Control so objects are inaccessible directly. A practical use case is a subscription video service: after verifying a subscriber, your server generates a signed URL or sets a signed cookie so the viewer can stream for a limited window. Beware of clock skew and make expiration times conservative; also do not embed private keys in client-side code. The core trade-off is between convenience and tight control: signed cookies ease multi-object access, signed URLs give stricter per-object control. Signed URLs and Signed Cookies for restricted content means use signed urls for single-object temporary access and signed cookies for session-based multi-object access while keeping the origin private.. In practical terms, grant time-limited access to private objects without making the origin public. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Security Signed URLs & Cookies
Signed URLs and signed cookies
Grant temporary access to private content without opening the origin to the public.
Signed URL
One URL signed with an expiration time. Use for single downloads or video links that must expire.
Signed Cookie
Set cookies that grant the browser access to multiple restricted resources without signing each file separately.
Practical guidance
  • Sign on the server after authenticating the user and include a short expiration time.
  • Keep signing keys secure; never expose them client-side.
  • Combine with Origin Access Control so the origin remains private.

screens.title: Programmatic management and CI/CD integration
screens.narratorSegment: Programmatically managing CloudFront distributions is essential for repeatable deployments. Use the AWS SDK or CLI to create distributions, update cache behaviors, and issue invalidations as part of your CI/CD pipeline. For example, after building and uploading static assets to S3, a pipeline step can create invalidation requests for changed files so users receive the new assets quickly. The Python example earlier is a common pattern: call create_invalidation with the distribution ID and a list of paths. When automating distribution updates, consider the propagation time for changes—some updates take minutes to deploy. screens.title: Common mistakes and cost considerations
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring pitfalls when using CloudFront that cost performance, money, or security. The most common operational mistake is over-invalidating — issuing broad invalidations such as /* frequently will force CloudFront to refetch many objects, eliminate the benefit of caching, and can incur additional invalidation charges. Prefer targeted invalidations or filename versioning for static assets. Second, misconfiguring cache keys by forwarding unnecessary headers or cookies fragments the cache and lowers hit ratios; forward only the headers and cookies your origin needs. Third, forgetting to lock down the origin is a security gap: if S3 is public, users can bypass CloudFront and avoid WAF rules or signed URLs. When using an ALB origin check security groups and network ACLs so CloudFront can reach the origin. Finally, neglecting propagation time for distribution configuration changes can lead to confusing troubleshooting; allow time for deployment and monitor the distribution's status. Planning your caching strategy and automating the careful invalidation of only what changed will keep cost and performance predictable. screens.title: Real-world scenario: Marketing team updates and invalidation strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Imagine your marketing team uploads new hero images daily and deploys promotional JavaScript frequently. If you set long TTLs to maximize cache hits, users may continue to see old banners after an update. The correct response is to use targeted invalidations for those changed assets or to adopt filename versioning so each new asset appears as a new URL. Targeted invalidations might include paths like /banners/summer-2026. jpg or /promo/js/*. Broad invalidations like /* should be avoided except for exceptional situations because they force edges to fetch large volumes of content, increasing origin load and potentially cost. Another approach is to set shorter TTLs for marketing assets that change often while leaving core framework files on long TTLs. In practical deployments you will often use a combination: version core assets, set long TTLs, and create narrow invalidations for marketing updates. This strategy keeps performance high while allowing rapid content updates when necessary. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the core terms to carry forward. A Content Delivery Network, or CDN, is a distributed network of edge caches that serves content closer to users for better latency and availability. A CloudFront distribution defines how content is delivered — it connects viewers to one or more origins and contains behaviors that route and cache requests per path pattern. Edge locations are the global sites where CloudFront stores cached objects. An origin is the source of truth for content, such as an S3 bucket or an ALB. Behaviors determine caching, allowed methods, and protocol policies for URL patterns. Cache invalidation is the mechanism to remove objects from edge caches before their TTL expires so fresh content is fetched on the next request. Signed URLs and signed cookies control temporary access to private content without making origins public. Origin Access Control ensures S3 objects are available only through CloudFront. Keep these concepts in mind as you design delivery, caching, and access control for your applications.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn what a Content Delivery Network does and why Amazon CloudFront is the CDN you use to reduce latency and protect origins. You will understand how edge locations cache content to serve users from nearby points of presence, and how a CloudFront distribution ties origins, behaviors, caching, and security together. We'll compare common origins like S3 and an Application Load Balancer, and you will see practical reasons to use behaviors to separate caching rules for static assets versus A P I traffic. I will also explain best practices for maintaining freshness: cache headers, targeted invalidations, and when to avoid over-invalidating. Security is part of the value proposition — CloudFront integrates with AWS Certificate Manager for TLS, with AWS WAF for filtering, and offers signed URLs and signed cookies to control access. Finally, we'll preview programmatic control using the AWS SDK to automate invalidations inside a CI/CD pipeline. By the end you should be able to plan a CloudFront integration that improves performance, reduces origin load, and keeps private content secure.

These objectives frame practical outcomes you should achieve. First, you'll be able to explain what a CDN does and why CloudFront reduces latency and origin load; this includes identifying edge locations and how they cache content. Second, you will configure a CloudFront distribution with multiple origins such as an S3 bucket, an Application Load Balancer, or a custom HTTP server, and create behaviors that route different URL paths to different origins with appropriate caching and protocol policies. Third, you'll implement cache strategies and invalidation techniques to balance freshness and performance, learning when to set TTLs and when to perform targeted invalidations. Finally, you will secure a distribution using TLS from AWS Certificate Manager, protect routes with AWS WAF, and implement signed URLs or signed cookies for restricted content. Each objective supports a verified competency milestone so you can measure readiness and integrate these steps into CI/CD automation. These outcomes are practical and map directly to hands-on tasks you will perform in the lab.

This second objectives screen zooms into practical skills you'll practice. You will configure behaviors to treat static and dynamic content differently: for example, set long TTLs for images served from S3 while forwarding all headers and using minimal caching for A P I routes served by an ALB. You will learn to set viewer protocol policies so users are redirected to HTTPS, and to attach AWS WAF rules to filter malicious requests. You will also implement Origin Access Control on an S3 origin to prevent direct access and ensure all requests pass through CloudFront. Finally, you'll script invalidations using the AWS SDK so deployments trigger targeted cache refreshes. Practically, you will be able to decide when to invalidate specific object paths and when to rely on TTLs and cache-control headers to preserve cache benefits. These skills reduce latency, increase security, and help keep a predictable deployment lifecycle.

A CDN is a distributed system that stores copies of content closer to users to lower latency and handle more traffic without overwhelming the origin. In CloudFront, those caches live at edge locations worldwide. Think of a CDN like a network of neighborhood libraries: instead of every reader traveling to a single central archive, the city keeps copies nearby so most readers get instant access. For a developer this matters because your static assets—images, stylesheets, scripts—and even some dynamic responses can be served directly from those edge caches. That reduces round-trip time, speeds page loads, and lowers origin costs. A clear example: a user in Tokyo requesting an image stored in an S3 bucket in Virginia will be served from the nearest edge if cached, avoiding the transoceanic trip to the origin. A common misconception is that CDNs always serve the latest version; they do not unless you configure short TTLs or invalidate items. TTLs and cache-control headers control freshness, so plan for update workflows, staging, and invalidation as part of your deployment process. Remember that a CDN is not just performance—it's also a layer where security and request filtering can be applied before origin resources are touched.

A CloudFront distribution is the configuration object that connects viewers to origins. Each distribution can have multiple origins: think of an S3 bucket for static files, an Application Load Balancer for dynamic application traffic, and even a custom HTTP server. Behaviors define which origin serves a given URL path and which caching settings apply. For example, a behavior for /images/* can point to an S3 origin with long TTLs and allow only GET and HEAD methods, while /api/* maps to an ALB with all methods allowed and minimal caching. Viewer protocol policy within a behavior enforces whether HTTP requests are redirected to HTTPS. Origin request policies let you control which headers, cookies, and query strings CloudFront forwards to the origin — this affects cache key granularity. A practical rule: keep cache keys as small as possible to increase cache hit rates. Also, when an ALB or EC2 is used as an origin, verify security group and network rules so CloudFront can reach the origin. This architecture separates static and dynamic concerns while improving global performance and operational control. CloudFront distribution, origins, and behaviors means a distribution ties multiple origins to path-based behaviors, each with its own caching and protocol rules.. In practical terms, how distributions map user requests to the right origin and caching policy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Caching strategy is the set of decisions that determine how long objects remain in edge caches and when to fetch fresh content from an origin. CloudFront uses cache policies and origin headers to build cache keys and set TTL behavior. Start by choosing what to include in the cache key: ideally, keep it minimal so more requests match the same cache entry. Headers, cookies, and query strings can be forwarded selectively; forward only what your origin needs. TTLs are defined as minimum, default, and maximum values in cache policies. Use long TTLs for versioned static assets and shorter TTLs for frequently changing resources. Set Cache-Control and Expires headers on the origin to communicate freshness; CloudFront honors those unless overridden by distribution cache policy. A common workflow is to deploy new static files with versioned filenames, set long TTLs, and then avoid invalidations. When you cannot version, use targeted invalidations for changed paths. A common pitfall is over-broad forwarding of headers or caching keys leading to cache fragmentation and poor hit ratio. Balance precision and simplicity to maximize cache effectiveness and reduce origin load.

Cache invalidation forces CloudFront to remove specified objects from edge caches before their TTL expires so that subsequent requests fetch the updated content from the origin. Use invalidations sparingly and target specific paths to preserve cache benefits. A common automated pattern is to call the SDK as part of a CI/CD pipeline after deploying new static assets. These are the core terms to carry forward. A Content Delivery Network, or CDN, is a distributed network of edge caches that serves content closer to users for better latency and availability. A CloudFront distribution defines how content is delivered — it connects viewers to one or more origins and contains behaviors that route and cache requests per path pattern. Edge locations are the global sites where CloudFront stores cached objects. An origin is the source of truth for content, such as an S3 bucket or an ALB. Behaviors determine caching, allowed methods, and protocol policies for URL patterns. Cache invalidation is the mechanism to remove objects from edge caches before their TTL expires so fresh content is fetched on the next request. Signed URLs and signed cookies control temporary access to private content without making origins public. Origin Access Control ensures S3 objects are available only through CloudFront. Keep these concepts in mind as you design delivery, caching, and access control for your applications.

These three quick cards lock in the practical items you will use when designing CloudFront deployments. First, a Distribution is the CloudFront resource that maps viewers to one or more origins and defines behaviors for caching and protocol policies. Second, a Behavior is a rule inside a distribution that controls which origin handles a request and how CloudFront caches it, including methods and forwarded values. Third, Cache Invalidation is the operation that removes objects from edge caches before their TTL expires and is commonly used sparingly after deployments to ensure freshness. Keep this trio in mind: define distributions carefully, create behaviors that reflect content patterns, and use invalidation judiciously or prefer asset versioning.
